Fact: Believers met on the first day of the week to break bread and set aside their giving, marking the day of the resurrection. Sunday worship is one of the earliest distinctly Christian customs.

Title: Baptism was by immersion into a death
Fact: Paul describes baptism as being buried with Christ and raised to new life. The imagery of going down and coming up shaped the practice in the earliest centuries.

Title: Communion was a meal with a warning
Fact: The Corinthians turned the Lord's Supper into a meal where the rich ate first and the poor went hungry, and Paul rebuked them sharply. The sacrament was inseparable from how the community treated its poorest members.

Title: An early creed quoted by Paul
Fact: Paul says he passed on what he received about Christ's death, burial, resurrection, and appearances. Scholars date this formula to within a few years of the events themselves.

Title: An early hymn about humility
Fact: The passage about Christ emptying himself and taking the form of a servant has the rhythm of a hymn Paul was quoting. Christians were singing about the incarnation within decades of it.

Title: Elders and overseers were appointed locally
Fact: Paul and Barnabas appointed elders in each church with prayer and fasting before moving on. Local leadership, not permanent missionary control, was the plan from the start.

Title: Character mattered more than charisma
Fact: The qualifications for church leadership are mostly about character: hospitality, self-control, gentleness, sound family life, and a good reputation with outsiders. Only one item on the list, being able to teach, is a skill.

Title: Widows had an organised order
Fact: The early church kept a list of widows supported by the congregation, with guidelines about who should be enrolled. Structured Christian social care is visible already in the first century.

Title: Slaves and masters addressed in one room
Fact: Paul addressed masters and slaves in the same letters, telling masters they had a Master in heaven who shows no favouritism. Both groups were present when the letters were read aloud.

Title: A letter about a runaway slave
Fact: Philemon is a personal note asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus back as a beloved brother. Abolitionists later used the letter heavily in their arguments.

Title: Prayer for governing authorities
Fact: Christians were told to pray for kings and all in authority, including the emperors who persecuted them. Prayers for rulers remain part of most Christian liturgies today.

Title: All have sinned
Fact: Paul's argument in Romans levels every distinction by saying all have sinned and fall short of God's glory. The verse is the hinge between his indictment and his account of grace.

Title: Wages versus gift
Fact: Paul contrasts the wages of sin with the free gift of God, using the language of a pay packet against a present. Nothing in the sentence is earned on the second side.

Title: Love demonstrated before we were ready
Fact: Romans says God demonstrated his love in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. The timing, not the act alone, is Paul's point.

Title: The good I want to do
Fact: Paul describes doing the very thing he hates and failing to do the good he wants. Christians in every century have recognised their own inner conflict in that passage.

Title: No condemnation
Fact: Romans 8 opens by declaring there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. It is one of the most quoted verses in Christian counselling and pastoral care.

Title: The Spirit prays when words fail
Fact: Paul says the Spirit intercedes with groanings too deep for words when we do not know what to pray. Christian teaching on prayer treats inarticulate prayer as still real prayer.

Title: All things work together
Fact: Romans promises that God works all things together for good for those who love him, without claiming all things are good. The distinction has mattered enormously in Christian grief.

Title: Nothing can separate us
Fact: Paul lists death, life, angels, rulers, height, depth, and anything in creation as unable to separate believers from God's love. The list reads like a deliberate attempt to leave no loophole.

Title: Faith comes by hearing
Fact: Paul argues that faith comes from hearing the message about Christ, which is why he insists on sending preachers. The verse has motivated evangelism and radio missions alike.

Title: Worship as an offering of the body
Fact: Paul calls offering your body as a living sacrifice your true and proper worship. Worship in the New Testament is defined by daily life before it is defined by singing.

Title: Do not be conformed
Fact: Christians are told not to be conformed to this age but transformed by the renewing of the mind. Both verbs are passive, describing pressure from outside and change from within.

Title: Weep with those who weep
Fact: Paul instructs believers to rejoice with the joyful and weep with the weeping, matching another person's emotional state. Christian comfort begins with presence rather than explanation.

Title: Overcome evil with good
Fact: Paul tells Christians never to repay evil for evil and to overcome evil with good, quoting Proverbs about feeding a hungry enemy. Non-retaliation was one of the most noticed early Christian traits.

Title: Limiting your freedom for others
Fact: Paul argued that believers should restrain their liberty rather than cause a weaker believer to stumble. Christian ethics includes considering effects on others, not only permissibility.

Title: The cross looks foolish by design
Fact: Paul admits the message of the cross seems foolish to those perishing and a stumbling block to many. He does not adjust the message to fix the impression.

Title: God chooses the overlooked
Fact: Paul notes that not many of the Corinthians were wise, powerful, or nobly born, and that God chose the weak things. Early Christianity spread substantially among ordinary and marginal people.

Title: The body belongs to God
Fact: Paul tells the Corinthians their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they were bought at a price. Christian sexual ethics in that letter is grounded in worth, not in shame.

Title: A way out of temptation
Fact: Paul promises that no temptation is beyond the common human experience and that God provides a way of escape. The verse assumes temptation is normal rather than a sign of failure.

Title: Whatever you do, do it for God's glory
Fact: Paul applies this even to eating and drinking, the most ordinary daily acts. It is the clearest New Testament statement that there is no secular category of life.

Title: Different gifts, one Spirit
Fact: Paul lists varieties of gifts, service, and activity all traced to the same Spirit. Diversity in the church is presented as intentional design rather than tolerated difference.

Title: The eye cannot say to the hand
Fact: Paul argues that no part of the body can tell another that it is unnecessary, and that weaker parts are indispensable. The image was aimed at a congregation ranking each other by spiritual gifts.

Title: The love chapter was written to a divided church
Fact: The passage read at countless weddings was addressed to people arguing about status and gifts. Love is described mostly by what it does and does not do rather than by what it feels.

Title: Seeing in a mirror dimly
Fact: Paul compares present knowledge to a polished bronze mirror's blurred reflection, promising clarity later. Ancient mirrors were metal, so the image was sharper for its first readers.

Title: Order in worship
Fact: Paul concludes his instructions about chaotic gatherings by saying everything should be done decently and in order. Christian liturgy grew partly from this insistence on intelligibility.

Title: If Christ is not raised
Fact: Paul states that if the resurrection did not happen, Christian preaching and faith are useless and believers are to be pitied. Few religions stake everything so explicitly on a historical event.

Title: Comfort passed along
Fact: Paul says God comforts us in our troubles so that we can comfort others with the comfort we received. Christian care ministry often traces its rationale to this verse.

Title: Treasure in clay jars
Fact: Paul compares believers to cheap clay pots holding great treasure so the power is clearly God's. Ordinary pottery was the disposable packaging of the ancient world.

Title: Ambassadors of reconciliation
Fact: Paul describes Christians as ambassadors through whom God makes his appeal. The image implies representing someone else's interests in a foreign place.

Title: Cheerful giving, not reluctant
Fact: Paul says each should give what they have decided in their heart, not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver. The Greek word for cheerful is the root of the English word hilarious.

Title: Strength made perfect in weakness
Fact: Paul asked three times for his thorn in the flesh to be removed and was told God's grace was sufficient. He then said he would boast about his weaknesses instead.

Title: Paul confronted Peter publicly
Fact: Paul opposed Peter to his face at Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile meals under pressure. The New Testament preserves a conflict between two of its greatest leaders.

Title: Neither Jew nor Greek
Fact: Paul declared that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female. The statement was radical in a world organised entirely by those categories.

Title: The fruit of the Spirit is singular
Fact: Paul lists love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control as one fruit, not nine. They are presented as growing together rather than being chosen individually.

Title: Carry each other's burdens
Fact: Paul instructs believers to restore someone caught in sin gently and to carry one another's burdens. Restoration, not exclusion, is the stated goal.

Title: Saved by grace through faith
Fact: Ephesians states that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so no one can boast. The next verse immediately calls believers God's workmanship, created for good works.

Title: Dividing walls broken down
Fact: Paul describes Christ destroying the barrier of hostility between Jew and Gentile, likely alluding to the temple wall Gentiles could not pass. Archaeologists have found warning inscriptions from that very barrier.

Title: Do not let the sun go down on anger
Fact: Paul allows for anger but sets a deadline on it and warns against giving the devil a foothold. Anger is treated as dangerous mainly when it is nursed.

Title: Speech that builds up
Fact: Christians are told to let no unwholesome talk come out of their mouths but only what builds others up according to their need. Speech ethics take up a striking amount of New Testament attention.

Title: The armour of God is mostly defensive
Fact: Of the six pieces Paul lists, only the sword of the Spirit is an offensive weapon. He drew the image from the Roman soldiers who likely guarded him.

Title: Rejoice always, written from prison
Fact: Philippians, the most joyful of Paul's letters, was written while he was in custody awaiting a verdict. Joy in that letter is explicitly not dependent on circumstances.

Title: Anxiety answered with thanksgiving
Fact: Paul pairs the instruction not to be anxious with prayer, petition, and thanksgiving, promising a peace that guards the heart. Gratitude is prescribed as part of the remedy.

Title: Contentment is learned
Fact: Paul says he has learned to be content whether well fed or hungry, in plenty or in want. He presents contentment as a skill acquired over time, not a temperament.

Title: Think about such things
Fact: Paul directs attention to whatever is true, noble, right, pure, lovely, and admirable. Christian teaching on mental habits has drawn on this verse for centuries.

Title: Work as if for the Lord
Fact: Colossians tells slaves and workers to do their work heartily as for the Lord rather than for people. The verse later shaped Protestant teaching that ordinary jobs are genuine vocations.

Title: Clothe yourselves with compassion
Fact: Paul uses the image of getting dressed for compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, with love as the outer garment. Character is described as something deliberately put on each day.

Title: Pray without ceasing
Fact: Paul's shortest instructions tell believers to rejoice always, pray continually, and give thanks in all circumstances. Monastic traditions of constant prayer grew directly from this verse.

Title: Test everything, hold on to the good
Fact: Paul tells the Thessalonians not to treat prophecies with contempt but to test them all and keep what is good. Discernment rather than blanket acceptance or rejection is the instruction.

Title: Grief with hope
Fact: Paul does not tell bereaved Christians to avoid grief but not to grieve like those without hope. Christian funerals have held sorrow and hope together on the strength of this distinction.

Title: A rule about work and food
Fact: Paul instructed that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, addressing people who had stopped working while awaiting Christ's return. The saying is about idleness, not inability.

Title: Do not grow weary in doing good
Fact: Paul's closing charge to the Thessalonians is not to tire of doing what is right. Endurance, not intensity, is the quality most often urged in his letters.

Title: Scripture is described as God-breathed
Fact: Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, correction, and training. When he wrote it, the Scripture he meant was primarily the Old Testament.

Title: Pass it on to faithful people
Fact: Paul told Timothy to entrust what he had heard to reliable people who would teach others. Four generations of discipleship appear in a single sentence.

Title: Do not let anyone despise your youth
Fact: Paul urged the young Timothy to set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity instead of arguing about his age. Credibility is answered with character.

Title: The love of money, not money
Fact: The famous line says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, not that money itself is evil. Paul's instruction to the rich is to be generous and ready to share.

Title: Paul asked for his cloak and his books
Fact: In what may be his last letter, Paul asked Timothy to bring his cloak, his scrolls, and especially the parchments. Even facing execution he wanted something to read.

Title: Grace trains us
Fact: Titus describes grace as a teacher that trains believers to say no to ungodliness and live self-controlled lives. Grace is presented as formative rather than merely forgiving.

Title: Jesus called our brother
Fact: Hebrews says Jesus is not ashamed to call those he makes holy his brothers and sisters. The letter's central argument is that he shared fully in human experience.

Title: A high priest who understands
Fact: Hebrews says we do not have a high priest unable to sympathise with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every way. Approaching God with confidence is grounded in that shared experience.

Title: Faith defined
Fact: Hebrews 11 defines faith as confidence in what is hoped for and assurance about what is not seen, then gives a long roll call of examples. The list includes people whose lives were messy and unfinished.

Title: A great cloud of witnesses
Fact: Hebrews pictures previous generations of the faithful as spectators in a stadium while believers run their race. The image encourages endurance by placing the present in a long line.

Title: Do not neglect meeting together
Fact: Hebrews urges believers not to give up gathering, as some were in the habit of doing, but to spur one another on. Attendance problems in the church are almost two thousand years old.

Title: Jesus Christ the same yesterday and today
Fact: Hebrews closes with the claim that Christ does not change. The line has anchored Christian confidence through every century of upheaval since.

Title: Faith without works is dead
Fact: James insists that faith showing no evidence in action is lifeless, using the example of wishing a cold person well without giving clothing. He and Paul are answering different questions, not contradicting each other.

Title: Quick to listen, slow to speak
Fact: James pairs listening quickly with speaking slowly and becoming angry slowly. It is among the most practical single verses on conversation in Scripture.

Title: The tongue is a small fire
Fact: James compares the tongue to a ship's rudder, a horse's bit, and a spark that sets a forest ablaze. Three images in a row underline how much damage small words do.

Title: Religion God accepts
Fact: James defines pure religion as caring for orphans and widows in distress and keeping oneself unstained by the world. Practical care is named before personal purity.

Title: Do not show favouritism to the rich
Fact: James rebukes congregations for giving the well-dressed visitor a good seat while the poor man stands. Church seating is used as a test of whether the gospel has landed.

Title: Confession and prayer for the sick
Fact: James tells believers to call the elders to pray and anoint the sick with oil, and to confess sins to one another. Anointing the sick as a church practice comes largely from this passage.

Title: Always be ready to give a reason
Fact: Peter tells believers to be prepared to explain their hope, but to do it with gentleness and respect. The discipline of Christian apologetics takes both its name and its manners from this verse.

Title: A royal priesthood
Fact: Peter applies temple language to ordinary believers, calling them a chosen people and a royal priesthood. The idea of every believer as a priest later became a Reformation rallying point.

Title: Cast your anxiety on him
Fact: Peter tells scattered, suffering Christians to throw their worries onto God because he cares for them. The letter was written to people facing real social hostility.

Title: A thousand years like a day
Fact: Peter answers those mocking the delay of Christ's return by saying God reckons time differently and is patient, wanting people to repent. Delay is interpreted as mercy.

Title: God is light and God is love
Fact: John's first letter offers two short definitions of God: God is light, and God is love. It also says anyone who claims to love God while hating a brother is a liar.

Title: Confession and cleansing
Fact: John writes that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us. The verse is read in countless Christian services of confession each week.

Title: Love in action, not only words
Fact: John insists that love should be shown with actions and truth rather than with words and talk. The test he gives is whether someone with possessions helps a brother in need.

Title: Short letters to individuals
Fact: Second and Third John are single-page notes, and Third John concerns hospitality to travelling teachers and one man who refused to welcome them. Church conflict over hospitality is preserved in the canon.

Title: Contend for the faith
Fact: Jude says he intended to write about salvation but instead had to urge readers to contend for the faith entrusted to them. Even the reason for the letter's change of subject is preserved.

Title: Revelation was written to seven real churches
Fact: Before the visions, Revelation addresses seven named congregations in Asia Minor with specific praise and criticism. The cities sit along a genuine ancient postal route.

Title: A knock at the door
Fact: The image of Christ standing at the door and knocking was addressed to a lukewarm church, not to unbelievers. Holman Hunt's painting of the scene made it one of the best-known Christian images.

Title: A multitude no one could count
Fact: John sees a crowd from every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne. The vision of the redeemed is explicitly multi-ethnic.

Title: Every tear wiped away
Fact: Revelation promises a new creation where God wipes every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain are gone. Christian hope ends not with escape from the world but with its renewal.

Title: The Bible ends with a city, not a garden
Fact: Scripture opens in a garden and closes with a city where the tree of life grows and the nations are healed. Urban imagery carries the final vision of God's future.

Title: Rome noticed Christians early
Fact: Around AD 112 the governor Pliny the Younger wrote to Emperor Trajan describing Christians who met before dawn, sang to Christ as to a god, and bound themselves by oath to avoid theft, adultery, and fraud. The letter is one of the earliest outside descriptions of Christian worship.

Title: The fish symbol was an acrostic
Fact: The Greek word for fish, ichthys, formed the initials of the phrase 'Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour'. It appears scratched on walls and tombs from the second century onward.

Title: Catacomb art avoided the cross at first
Fact: Early Christian art in the Roman catacombs favoured images of the Good Shepherd, an anchor, and Jonah rather than crucifixion scenes. The cross was still an active instrument of execution and carried deep social shame.

Title: Christians rescued abandoned infants
Fact: Exposure of unwanted newborns was legal and common in the Roman Empire, and early Christians became known for collecting and raising those children. Church writers condemned the practice for centuries before Roman law did.

Title: Plague care changed public opinion
Fact: During the epidemics of the second and third centuries, Christians in cities like Alexandria stayed to nurse the sick, including non-Christians, while others fled. Historians point to this care as one reason the movement grew.

Title: Sunday was not a holiday at first
Fact: Before Constantine, Sunday was an ordinary working day, so Christians gathered before dawn or after work. The day off came only in AD 321 when Sunday was declared a day of rest in the empire.

Title: The canon was recognised, not invented
Fact: Lists of accepted New Testament books circulated from the second century, and the criteria were apostolic origin, wide use, and consistency with the faith. Athanasius listed the familiar twenty-seven books in a festal letter of AD 367.

Title: The Apostles' Creed grew from baptism
Fact: The creed developed out of the questions asked of candidates at baptism about belief in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Its three-part shape still follows that ancient interrogation.

Title: Nicaea addressed who Jesus is
Fact: The council of AD 325 at Nicaea affirmed that the Son is of the same substance as the Father, against the teaching of Arius. The resulting creed is still recited by most Christian traditions worldwide.

Title: Constantinople completed the creed
Fact: The council of AD 381 expanded the section on the Holy Spirit, producing the version most churches now call the Nicene Creed. Doctrinal clarity developed gradually in response to live disputes.

Title: Chalcedon defined two natures
Fact: In AD 451 the council at Chalcedon confessed Christ as fully God and fully human in one person, without confusion or division. The formula set boundaries rather than explaining the mystery.

Title: Monasticism began in the desert
Fact: Antony of Egypt withdrew to the desert around AD 270 after hearing a Gospel reading about selling possessions. The communities that followed preserved learning and Scripture for centuries.

Title: The Rule of Benedict balanced prayer and work
Fact: Written around AD 530, Benedict's rule organised monastic life around prayer, study, and manual labour in a moderate daily rhythm. Its motto of prayer and work shaped European culture for a thousand years.

Title: Jerome translated the Bible into Latin
Fact: Jerome spent decades producing the Latin Vulgate, working from Hebrew for the Old Testament rather than only from Greek. His translation was the standard Bible of Western Europe for over a millennium.

Title: Augustine wrote the first great memoir
Fact: Augustine's Confessions, written around AD 400, is often called the first Western autobiography and is addressed throughout to God. His restless heart line remains one of the most quoted sentences in Christian writing.

Title: Hospitals grew from Christian charity
Fact: Basil of Caesarea founded a complex around AD 370 with lodging for travellers, care for the sick, and a leper colony, staffed to serve anyone in need. Historians often identify it as an ancestor of the public hospital.

Title: Patrick returned to the place of his captivity
Fact: Patrick was taken to Ireland as a slave in his teens, escaped, and later returned as a missionary in the fifth century. His own short Confession is one of the earliest documents from the British Isles.

Title: Irish monks copied manuscripts by hand
Fact: Monasteries in Ireland and Northumbria produced illuminated Gospel books such as the Book of Kells, copying Scripture letter by letter. A single copy could take a scribe years of work.

Title: An alphabet invented for the Bible
Fact: In the ninth century the missionary brothers Cyril and Methodius created a written script so Slavic peoples could hear Scripture and worship in their own language. The Cyrillic alphabet still bears one of their names.

Title: East and West divided in 1054
Fact: Long-building disagreements over authority and a clause in the creed led to mutual excommunications between Rome and Constantinople. The separation between Catholic and Orthodox Christianity dates from that year.

Title: Cathedrals were built across generations
Fact: Medieval cathedrals often took more than a century to finish, so masons worked on buildings they would never see completed. Their stained glass told Bible stories to congregations who could not read.

Title: Francis gave away his inheritance
Fact: Francis of Assisi, son of a wealthy cloth merchant, renounced his family fortune around 1206 and lived among the poor and sick. He is also credited with setting up the first nativity scene, in 1223.

Title: Preaching orders went to the cities
Fact: The Dominicans and Franciscans of the thirteenth century broke with the monastic pattern by moving into towns to teach and serve among ordinary people. Urban mission is not a modern invention.

Title: Faith and reason argued together
Fact: Thomas Aquinas spent the thirteenth century arguing that reason and revelation cannot finally conflict because both come from God. His Summa Theologiae is still studied in philosophy departments.

Title: A woman theologian in a walled room
Fact: Julian of Norwich lived as an anchoress and wrote the earliest surviving book in English known to be by a woman, around 1395. Her line that all shall be well was written in a century of plague.

Title: Wycliffe pushed for an English Bible
Fact: John Wycliffe and his followers produced English translations from Latin in the 1380s, decades before printing. Church authorities condemned the work, and his bones were later dug up and burned.

Title: Jan Hus was burned for reform
Fact: The Czech preacher Jan Hus was executed in 1415 for criticising church corruption and insisting on Scripture's authority. Luther later said he had been a Hussite without knowing it.

Title: The first printed book was a Bible
Fact: Gutenberg's press produced its Latin Bible around 1455, and roughly forty-nine copies survive today. Printing made the Reformation's flood of pamphlets and Bibles possible within a single lifetime.

Title: Ninety-five theses for debate
Fact: Luther posted his theses in Wittenberg in October 1517 as an invitation to academic discussion about indulgences, written in Latin. Someone else translated and printed them in German, and they spread across Europe in weeks.

Title: Luther translated the New Testament in eleven weeks
Fact: While hiding in the Wartburg castle in 1521 and 1522, Luther translated the New Testament into German from Greek. His translation helped standardise the modern German language.

Title: Tyndale gave English its Bible vocabulary
Fact: William Tyndale coined phrases like 'the salt of the earth' and 'let there be light' in English, and was executed in 1536 for his translation work. Much of the King James Version retains his wording.

Title: Five Latin slogans summarise the Reformation
Fact: Scripture alone, faith alone, grace alone, Christ alone, and glory to God alone were later gathered as a summary of Reformation convictions. They function as a contrast set rather than a full theology.

Title: Congregational singing returned
Fact: Reformers restored singing to the whole congregation rather than only trained choirs, and Luther wrote hymns for ordinary people. 'A Mighty Fortress' is based on Psalm 46.

Title: Geneva became a refugee city
Fact: Under Calvin's influence from the 1540s, Geneva took in thousands of Protestant refugees and organised deacons' funds to support them. Church-run welfare structures were part of the reform, not an afterthought.

Title: Anabaptists insisted on believers' baptism
Fact: Sixteenth-century Anabaptists baptised adults on profession of faith and generally refused the sword, and were persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike. Mennonite, Amish, and Brethren traditions descend from them.

Title: The King James Version took seven years
Fact: Around forty-seven scholars worked in six committees from 1604 to 1611, revising earlier English translations rather than starting fresh. Its rhythms shaped English prose for three centuries.

Title: A prayer book shaped English worship
Fact: Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549, gave English-speaking Christians a common liturgy for worship, marriage, and burial. Phrases like 'till death us do part' come from it.

Title: Pilgrim's Progress was written in prison
Fact: John Bunyan wrote his allegory of the Christian life while jailed for preaching without a licence in the 1660s and 1670s. For two centuries it was the most widely read book in English after the Bible.

Title: Hymns were once controversial
Fact: Isaac Watts faced opposition in the early 1700s for writing new hymns rather than only singing metrical psalms. 'Joy to the World' and 'When I Survey the Wondrous Cross' are his.

Title: A method became a movement
Fact: John and Charles Wesley's Oxford group was mockingly called Methodist for its strict routine of study, prayer, fasting, and prison visiting. The nickname stuck and named a worldwide church family.

Title: Charles Wesley wrote thousands of hymns
Fact: Charles Wesley is credited with well over six thousand hymns, including 'Hark! the Herald Angels Sing' and 'And Can It Be'. Much of early Methodist theology was taught through singing.

Title: Preaching moved outdoors
Fact: George Whitefield and John Wesley preached in fields and marketplaces in the 1700s when pulpits were closed to them, reaching crowds of thousands. Open-air preaching reached miners and labourers who never entered a church.

Title: Amazing Grace was written by a slave trader
Fact: John Newton captained slave ships before his conversion and later became a clergyman who campaigned against the trade. He wrote the hymn for a New Year's service in 1773.

Title: Wilberforce fought for decades
Fact: William Wilberforce introduced abolition bills in Parliament year after year from 1789, driven openly by Christian conviction. He died days after the bill ending slavery in the British Empire passed in 1833.

Title: Sunday schools began as basic education
Fact: Robert Raikes started Sunday schools in Gloucester in 1780 to teach reading and writing to children working six days a week in factories. Literacy and Scripture were taught together.

Title: Expect great things, attempt great things
Fact: William Carey, a cobbler and pastor, sailed for India in 1793 and helped translate Scripture into dozens of Indian languages. He is often called the father of the modern missionary movement.

Title: A girl without a Bible started a society
Fact: Mary Jones walked some twenty-five miles in 1800 to buy a Welsh Bible she had saved six years for, and her story helped prompt the founding of the British and Foreign Bible Society. That society's model spread worldwide.

Title: An orphanage run on prayer alone
Fact: George Müller cared for more than ten thousand orphans in Bristol during the 1800s and made it his practice never to ask anyone directly for money. His detailed records of answered prayer fill several volumes.

Title: A missionary who wore Chinese dress
Fact: Hudson Taylor adopted Chinese clothing and customs in the 1850s against the expectations of other Western missionaries. His inland mission recruited workers who would live among the people they served.

Title: The Salvation Army began in the East End
Fact: William and Catherine Booth started work among the poorest of London in 1865, combining preaching with soup kitchens, shelters, and employment help. Catherine's preaching was central to the movement from the start.

Title: A blind hymn writer wrote thousands of texts
Fact: Fanny Crosby, blind from infancy, wrote some eight thousand hymn texts in the nineteenth century, including 'Blessed Assurance'. She also worked for years in rescue missions in New York.

Title: It Is Well was written after a shipwreck
Fact: Horatio Spafford wrote the hymn after his four daughters drowned in an Atlantic collision in 1873 and his wife cabled the words 'saved alone'. He is said to have written it while sailing past the place they died.

Title: Silent Night was first sung with a guitar
Fact: The carol was written in Austria in 1818 and first performed with guitar accompaniment, one account attributing this to a broken church organ. It is now sung in hundreds of languages each Christmas.

Title: Advent is a season of waiting
Fact: Advent covers the four Sundays before Christmas and was historically a time of preparation and fasting, not celebration. The wreath's candles mark the weeks of waiting for the light.

Title: Lent mirrors forty days in the wilderness
Fact: The forty days of Lent, excluding Sundays, recall Jesus' fasting before his ministry began. Fasting, prayer, and giving are its three traditional practices.

Title: Easter moves because it follows the moon
Fact: The Council of Nicaea tied Easter to the first Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox, keeping its link to Passover. That is why the date shifts each year.

Title: Grace before meals is an ancient habit
Fact: Jesus gave thanks before meals and the early church continued the Jewish practice of blessing God for food. The custom of saying grace has been unbroken in Christian homes for two thousand years.

Title: Church bells once ran daily life
Fact: For centuries bells called villages to prayer, marked deaths and weddings, and gave people the only public clock they had. Monastic hours of prayer set the rhythm of the day for whole communities.

Title: A pastor executed for resisting Hitler
Fact: Dietrich Bonhoeffer helped lead the Confessing Church against Nazi control of German Christianity and was hanged in April 1945, weeks before the war ended. His Cost of Discipleship warned against cheap grace.

Title: A watchmaker's family hid neighbours
Fact: Corrie ten Boom's family concealed Jewish neighbours in their Haarlem home during the Nazi occupation and were sent to concentration camps for it. She spent her later decades speaking about forgiveness.

Title: Scrolls found by a shepherd boy
Fact: The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered from 1947 in caves at Qumran, included Hebrew manuscripts a thousand years older than any previously known. The great Isaiah scroll showed remarkable agreement with the text used since.

Title: Widows returned to the tribe that killed their husbands
Fact: After five missionaries were speared in Ecuador in 1956, Elisabeth Elliot and Rachel Saint went to live among the same people. Several of the men involved later became Christians.

Title: Christianity's centre of gravity moved south
Fact: More Christians now live in Africa, Asia, and Latin America than in Europe and North America, a reversal that happened within a single century. Nigeria and Brazil today send missionaries to Europe.

Title: The Bible is still being translated
Fact: The full Bible exists in well over seven hundred languages and parts of it in more than three thousand, yet hundreds of languages still have none. Translation teams today are mostly led by native speakers.

Title: Persecution is not only ancient history
Fact: Christians continue to face imprisonment, restriction, or violence in dozens of countries today, and the New Testament letters were mostly written to communities in similar conditions. Hebrews tells believers to remember prisoners as though in prison with them.

Title: Ordinary faithfulness is the main story
Fact: For most of two thousand years, Christian life has been carried by unnamed people keeping promises, raising children, forgiving neighbours, and gathering weekly to worship. Paul's ambition for the church was that believers lead quiet lives, mind their own business, and work with their hands.
